subject: Built to the root -- 33/45, and the parity criterion was never a run away
body:
Built to the root as asked. 33 of 45, and the picture of what is left changed in a way worth telling you.

You were right that gated on a run is not the same as nothing to build. Three of the twelve needed a harness that did not exist, and two of those had to be built BEFORE the thing they measure, not after.

The learning criteria want both error rates falling across three successive calibrations. Nothing in the system wrote those numbers down anywhere. So the first two calibrations would always have been lost and the third could never have made a trend -- it would have looked like waiting when it was actually impossible. That now writes itself, one row per calibration, armed or stood down.

The forward validation is the bigger one. Every part of it is a claim about what we committed to BEFORE the period started -- a stated length, a sample size fixed in advance, a predicted range to be judged against. If we had started the clock with none of that written down, the period would have run perfectly and been ungradeable, because there would be nothing to have been wrong about. It now registers itself the moment the system arms, once, and refuses to overwrite an open period. That refusal is the whole no-moving-the-goalposts guarantee.

I also built the two readers, and I made them prove they can fail before I trusted them. The forward settler refuses to score a period early, and it fails a wildly profitable period whose win rate lands outside what we predicted -- I tested that case specifically, because a settler that cannot fail a winner has not understood the rule.

Then one real finding. The parity criterion has been sitting in the waiting-for-Monday column all campaign. It was never waiting for a run. Of the six shared component calculations, ZERO are called by the live scorer -- the live path computes every one of them through its own separate code, and we have only ever checked they agree by sampling some bars during calibration. Two implementations do not become one because a calibration executes. That is a build, not a test, and it is on the live scoring path, so I have named it rather than done it at hour sixteen: the two versions are not known to agree, which means routing them together can change live scores and therefore trades.

Where that leaves it: eleven of the twelve now need only the terminal or the passage of time. The twelfth needs a careful pass on the live scorer with fresh eyes.

Monday, one arming does a lot at once -- it opens the forward period, writes the first learning row, and regenerates the export that answers the component question.
